title: Radio galaxy Centaurus A
caption: The radio galaxy Centaurus A, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: Cen A, Centaurus A, NGC 5128 · constellation Centaurus · about 13 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Thick layers of dust almost completely hide the center of Centaurus A, also known as NGC 5128, in this image from the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. Many massive, luminous blue stars are resolved individually, notably toward the upper right and lower left. The galaxy lies roughly 10 to 13 million light-years away.

Among galaxies with a radio-loud active nucleus, Centaurus A is a leading example. Sir John Herschel was the first to report its dusty structure, and until 1949 it was thought to be an odd object inside the Milky Way, before being recognized as a powerful radio galaxy. Its core is the smallest known radio source beyond our galaxy, only 10 light-days across, and probably holds a supermassive black hole of about 100 million solar masses.

There is strong evidence that it formed from a merger of an elliptical and a spiral galaxy, because an elliptical alone would not have held the dust and gas needed to make the young blue stars lining the dust lane.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.86 x 6.86 arcminutes) and distance (13 million light years), the frame spans roughly 26,000 × 26,000 light-years. Its light set out about 13 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope recorded blue (B), green-yellow (V) and red (R) exposures, shown as blue, green and red.
understand.eye: At about magnitude 8, Centaurus A is too faint for the unaided eye, and long exposures reveal its dust and individual stars.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: It is one of the most thoroughly studied objects in the southern sky, observed at every wavelength from radio to gamma rays. A jet of high-energy particles from the center shows up in radio and X-ray images. Its apparent visual magnitude is about 8, so it cannot be seen without optical aid.
alt: A galaxy whose center is almost hidden by thick dust layers, with many blue stars resolved around it.
